title: AI is creating a 'human premium' for art made by people. But will it hold?
key_facts: A first-person BBC InDepth analysis by a DJ and writer asks whether audiences care if art is made by humans.

Deezer says 44% of tracks uploaded to it are AI-generated; its research found 97% of listeners could not tell AI music from other music, yet more than half of those surveyed said they care if it is made by AI.
Economist Daniel Susskind (King's College London) argues people value that a human hand made a work, as with chess after Deep Blue.
New Yorker journalist Kyle Chayka says readers are starting to value personal, messier writing because AI writing is seen as generic.
Academics are working on a universal ‘human made’ symbol, and ‘AI-free’ labels are appearing on some books, films and albums.
The author doubts the premium will hold: AI content is growing fast and people already accept algorithm-chosen culture.
Alex Mahon, chief executive of Superstruct Entertainment, notes growing appetite for live, in-person events.
quote_evidence: The music platform Deezer says 44% of tracks uploaded to it are AI-generated.
Its research also found that 97% of listeners couldn't tell what was AI-generated and what wasn't.
But here's a third statistic: more than half of those surveyed said they did care if it was made by AI.
why_it_matters_hint: Survey figures support the idea that audiences still want human-made art, but the author is unsure it will last.
